title: Sama's kindness
hookLine: the devoted son's kindness even to the king who shot him (Jataka 540)
tomorrow: a kind act every hour? at work, what even counts?

cards: When someone hurts you, the first sentence out of your mouth sets the whole next hour. Here's a first sentence from an old story, one that ends well.
A young man named Sama walks down to the river for water, and the deer walk with him, because they aren't afraid of him. His parents are blind, and he's the one who cares for them.
A king out hunting sees him and shoots before asking a single thing. The arrow lands. Sama sets down his water jar.
And the first thing he says isn't a curse. He asks who shot him, and why. No hate in it.

teach.h: THE KING PROMISES TO CARE FOR THEM.
teach.b: The king steps out, and Sama speaks to him gently. What worries him is his parents: they can't see, and they have no one else. The king is undone, and promises to care for them himself.

In the story, Sama falls still, and his parents and a goddess make solemn acts of truth over him, and he wakes. Tradition tells this as the life in which the Bodhisatta perfected loving-kindness. Kind even then.
But what does that ask of a person? Two answers live inside the tradition, and both are serious.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: THE SIMILE OF THE SAW.
teach.b: The first comes from the Simile of the Saw. The Buddha tells his monks that even if bandits were cutting them apart with a two-handled saw, anyone whose mind turned to hate would not be carrying out his teaching.
On this view, kindness is an inside job: no ill will, whatever happens. The second view points at Sama himself. He doesn't pretend nothing happened.

He tells the king plainly what he has done, and he asks for something: take care of my parents. Elsewhere the Buddha says he speaks what is true and helpful, even when it's unwelcome, if the time is right.
On this view, kindness can name the harm.

teach.h: A HEART THAT WON'T TURN; A TRUE VOICE.
teach.b: One stresses the heart that won't turn.
The other, the voice that still tells the truth.

how: The Sama Jataka is retold in Theravada Buddhist settings, in sermons, plays and temple paintings, as a story of loving-kindness and of caring for one's parents.

o: a prince's kindness to his loyal servants
goodwill toward the one who hurt him, with no hate
forgiveness offered once a hurt has healed

games.q: who's who by the river — tap the pairs.
p: no hate, even under the saw

s: being kind to someone who hurt you means pretending it didn't happen
Sama told the king plainly what he'd done, with no hate in it.
in the story, the king promises to care for Sama's parents
moved by Sama's gentleness, the king promises to look after them himself.
the Simile of the Saw says anger is fair if the harm is big enough
even under the saw, the Buddha says, a mind turned to hate isn't carrying out his teaching.

games.q: your cousin says "kind even then" means swallowing it and never saying a word. what's the best case for the other view?
o: Sama held no hate, and still told the king plainly what he'd done.
with someone who hurt you, a little anger is only fair.
the saw simile means you shouldn't feel anything at all.
games.why: both views are the tradition's own: the saw simile guards the heart; Sama's plain word shows kindness can still name the harm.

practice: Sit upright with one hand resting over your heart. Bring to mind someone who hurt you, a small hurt, not the biggest, and wish them one plain thing: may you be well.
If it sticks, wish yourself well for a while, then try them again.

wordCard.voice: Sama's kindness: goodwill that didn't turn, even toward the king who had just shot him, and still spoke the truth.

orig.note: Pali: the name of the devoted son in the Sama Jataka, Jataka 540.

carryVoice: Here's the line: kind even then, with no hate in it and a plain word ready. That's twenty-six.

sources.ref: Jataka 540, Sama Jataka (Sama shot by the hunting king; his gentleness; the king's promise; the acts of truth)
Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (the simile of the saw)
Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarajakumara Sutta (the Buddha speaks what is true and beneficial, even if unwelcome, knowing the right time)
